[Data Science]{.blue} ::: {.my-grey} [{{< meta semester >}} | {{< meta course >}}]{}
[Jeffrey M. Girard | Lecture {{< meta lecture >}}]{} ::: ![](../../img/proud_coder_357EDD.svg){.absolute bottom=30 right=0 width="400"} ::: ## Roadmap ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - Run correlation tests for continuous variables - Run Chi-Square tests for categorical variables ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/map.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Moving Beyond Groups {.smaller} Last lecture, we compared a continuous variable across different categories ::: {.fragment .mt1} - What if we want to test the association of [two continuous variables]{.b .blue}? + *e.g., As a penguin's flipper gets longer, does its body mass also increase?* + We can use **Correlation** to test this ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - What if we want to test the association of [two categorical variables]{.b .green}? + *e.g., Does the species of a penguin depend on which island it lives on?* + We can use **Chi-Square** to test this ::: # Correlations ## Interpreting Correlations {.smaller} - A correlation (parameter = $\rho$, statistic = $r$) quantifies the **direction** and **strength** of the *linear* relationship between two variables (how closely the points form a straight line) - [Hypotheses]{.b .dark-red}: + **$H_0$**: $\rho = 0$ (There is no linear relationship in the population) + **$H_1$**: $\rho \neq 0$ (There is a linear relationship in the population) - [Direction]{.b .blue}: do the variables change together or opposing? + $r > 0$: the variables change together + $r < 0$: the variables change in opposition - [Strength]{.b .green}: how well does one variable predict the other? + $r \to 0$: no linear relationship (but maybe a non-linear one) + $r \to \pm 1$: perfect (positive or negative) linear relationship ## Positive linear ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Negative linear ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## No linear / Nonlinear ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## 1. Preparing the Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(easystats) data("penguins", package = "datasets") dat1 <- penguins |> select(flipper_len, body_mass) glimpse(dat1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 344 Columns: 2 $ flipper_len 181, 186, 195, NA, 193, 190, 181, 195, 193, 190, 186, 180,… $ body_mass 3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250, … ``` ::: ::: ## 2. Exploring our Sample ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(dat1, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.6) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "salmon") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## 3. The Correlation Test ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res1 <- correlation(dat1) |> print() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # Correlation Matrix (pearson-method) Parameter1 | Parameter2 | r | 95% CI | t(340) | p ------------------------------------------------------------------- flipper_len | body_mass | 0.87 | [0.84, 0.89] | 32.72 | < .001*** p-value adjustment method: Holm (1979) Observations: 342 ``` ::: ::: :::{.fsmaller} **Interpretation:** The correlation ($r$) is 0.87. The significant result (*p* < .001) provides evidence that flipper length and body mass are positively associated in the population: penguins with more (or less) body mass tend to have longer (or shorter) flippers. ::: ## 4. Multiple Variables ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat2 <- penguins |> select(bill_len, bill_dep, flipper_len, body_mass) res2 <- correlation(dat2, p_adjust = "holm") |> print() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # Correlation Matrix (pearson-method) Parameter1 | Parameter2 | r | 95% CI | t(340) | p ----------------------------------------------------------------------- bill_len | bill_dep | -0.24 | [-0.33, -0.13] | -4.46 | < .001*** bill_len | flipper_len | 0.66 | [ 0.59, 0.71] | 16.03 | < .001*** bill_len | body_mass | 0.60 | [ 0.52, 0.66] | 13.65 | < .001*** bill_dep | flipper_len | -0.58 | [-0.65, -0.51] | -13.26 | < .001*** bill_dep | body_mass | -0.47 | [-0.55, -0.39] | -9.87 | < .001*** flipper_len | body_mass | 0.87 | [ 0.84, 0.89] | 32.72 | < .001*** p-value adjustment method: Holm (1979) Observations: 342 ``` ::: ::: ## 4. The Correlation Matrix ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mat2 <- summary(res2) |> print() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # Correlation Matrix (pearson-method) Parameter | body_mass | flipper_len | bill_dep ------------------------------------------------ bill_len | 0.60*** | 0.66*** | -0.24*** bill_dep | -0.47*** | -0.58*** | flipper_len | 0.87*** | | p-value adjustment method: Holm (1979) ``` ::: ::: :::{.fsmaller} **Interpretation:** The function automatically tests every possible pair of variables and provides adjusted $p$-values for each relationship. ::: ## 5. Visualizing the Matrix ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(mat2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Two Categorical Variables ## Understanding Chi-Square {.smaller} The **Chi-Square $(\chi^2)$ Test of Independence** looks at categorical relationships ::: {.fragment .mt1} - **The Core Question:** + Does knowing one category tell us something about the other category? + *e.g., Are the Species and Island categorical variables associated?* ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - **The Hypotheses:** + **Null Hypothesis ($H_0$):** The variables are completely independent + *e.g., species are randomly distributed across islands* + **Alternative Hypothesis ($H_1$):** The variables are associated + *e.g., some species are more common on some islands* ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - **The Data:** + We look at **frequencies** (counts) of each combination of categories ::: ## 1. Preparing the Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data("penguins", package = "datasets") dat3 <- penguins |> select(species, island) glimpse(dat3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 344 Columns: 2 $ species Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie… $ island Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgers… ``` ::: ::: ## 2. Exploring our Sample ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(dat3, aes(x = island, fill = species)) + geom_bar(position = "fill") + # "fill" makes all bars the same height labs(y = "Proportion") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## 3. Cross-Tabulation ::: {.fsmaller} Before we can test these variables, we need to count how many penguins fall into each combination of categories. We use the `xtabs()` function for this The syntax uses a one-sided formula `~ variable1 + variable2` ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tab3 <- dat3 |> table() |> print() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` island species Biscoe Dream Torgersen Adelie 44 56 52 Chinstrap 0 68 0 Gentoo 124 0 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fsmaller} **Note:** All Gentoo penguins were observed on Biscoe, and all Chinstrap penguins were observed on Dream This suggests a very strong association! ::: ::: ## 4. The Logic of Chi-Square {.smaller} How does a Chi-Square test actually work? - It compares what we **observed** in our data to what we would **expect** to see if the two variables were completely independent. - If species and island were unrelated, penguins would be distributed across the islands purely based on the overall size of each island and the overall population of each species. - The larger the difference between Observed and Expected, the larger our resulting Chi-Square statistic ($\chi^2$). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res3 <- chisq.test(tab3) ``` ::: ## 5. Expected Frequencies ::: {.fsmaller} R can calculate those "Expected" numbers for us, and we can compare them ::: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res3$observed ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` island species Biscoe Dream Torgersen Adelie 44 56 52 Chinstrap 0 68 0 Gentoo 124 0 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res3$expected ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` island species Biscoe Dream Torgersen Adelie 74.23256 54.79070 22.97674 Chinstrap 33.20930 24.51163 10.27907 Gentoo 60.55814 44.69767 18.74419 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fsmaller} **Note:** These tables are very different! If there were no association, we would expect to find about 45 Gentoo on Dream. But in our sample, we found 0 ::: ## 6. The Chi-Square Test :::{.fsmaller} Now we look at the formal test results using `model_parameters()` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model_parameters(res3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pearson's Chi-squared test Chi2(4) | p ---------------- 299.55 | < .001 ``` ::: ::: :::{.fsmaller} **Interpretation:** The highly significant result (*p* < .001) means the distribution of species is dependent on the island. We have strong evidence that this geographic sorting exists in the broader population. ::: ## 7. Effect Size ::: {.fsmaller} To quantify the *strength* of the association, we can calculate **Cramer's V** ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} effectsize(res3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Cramer's V (adj.) | 95% CI -------------------------------- 0.66 | [0.59, 1.00] - One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00]. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fsmaller} **Interpretation:** Cramer's V ranges from 0 to 1. A value of 0.84 indicates a very strong association between species and island location. ::: # Wrap-Up ## Choosing the Right Test {.smaller} You now have three primary tools for testing basic bivariate relationships

| Variable 1 | Variable 2 | Test | R Function | |:---|:---|:---|:---| | Categorical | Continuous | **ANOVA** | `aov_ez()` | | Continuous | Continuous | **Correlation** | `correlation()` | | Categorical | Categorical | **Chi-Square** | `chisq.test()` |

*Note: "Bivariate" means we are only looking at two variables at a time.
In future courses, you will learn how to build models with many variables!*

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
